source.title: A Geometric Unification of Concept Learning with Concept Cones
source.authors: Alexandre Rocchi-Henry; Thomas Fel; Gianni Franchi

page_placements.theme: Reconstruction and proxy metrics do not establish semantic recovery

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how SAE directions align with supervised concept directions and refines the interpretation of SAE features as semantic units: CBMs are partial anchors, and alignment depends on SAE choices. It does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE–CBM alignment measurements on vision models, not language models or toy networks. Cited statements about SAE instability are not new results from this study. The main text's flattened Table 1 is not assigned model-level values here. Rows focus on alignment measures that bear on whether SAE directions act as complete, canonical concept units; CBM classification results and other results not measuring that correspondence are omitted.
record.test_reason: In vision backbones (ResNet-50, ViT, DINOv2), the study measures how fully trained SAE dictionaries recover supervised human-concept directions, and how this changes with SAE variant, sparsity, expansion and layer. That bears on V5's completeness and canonicality, in a new setting and with a partial reference (CBMs), not ground truth. It does not test toy models (V1), the cause of polysemanticity (V2, V3), LLMs (V4) or feature dimensionality (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Additions: trained SAEs beat random SAEs on every metric except coverage, which a random cone inflates. Jump and Vanilla SAEs give the best coverage. Intermediate sparsity and about 2× expansion form a 'sweet spot'. Deeper ResNet layers align best with CBM semantics. The authors frame CBMs as partial anchors, not ground truth.
record.recipe_differences: This is a vision-model study comparing SAE dictionaries with CBM directions through cone, geometric, activation, coverage, and prediction metrics; it does not reproduce the toy-model interventions or measurements in Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported SAE–CBM alignment changes with SAE variant, target sparsity, expansion factor, layer, and the number and training strategy of CBM reference concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: Random, untrained SAE dictionaries reach higher CBM coverage than trained ones (0.65 vs 0.25 on CUB-R50). The authors attribute this to a larger, more dispersed cone; trained SAEs score higher on R2, F1 and ρuni.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cone or coverage-style measures of SAE concept recovery are confounded by dictionary dispersion, so random dictionaries can appear more complete.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparsity and expansion trade off: denser codes and larger dictionaries raise coverage and R2 but lower ρgeom and ρact.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE hyperparameters trade concentration of individual atoms against completeness of concept recovery.

record.problems: The paper states that CBM concepts are not complete ground truth and are limited by the vocabulary, annotations, and human choices. Alignment metrics are diagnostic proxies and can disagree; random SAEs can have artificially high coverage. The reported comparison therefore does not establish canonicality or complete feature recovery. The text gives results over three seeds for many tables, but the selected Table A.10 and A.11 values do not report uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports more alignment outcomes than can be fully represented under the 60-row cap. Omitted: the remaining metrics (including R2 and F1) for the SAE-variant comparisons in Table 2; the other backbones and ImageNet conditions in Tables A.4 and A.6; layer-wise rows in Table A.5; CBM-variant comparisons in Table A.9; and trained/random cone comparisons in Table A.8. These contain additional measures or settings of the same SAE–CBM alignment analysis. The main-text Table 1 was not separately extracted because its flattened layout does not reliably assign all values to model and metric columns.

untested.parts: Stability of features across seeds or independent SAE runs (instability is only cited). Canonicality against ground-truth features. Completeness beyond the CBM concept vocabulary. Causal role of features.
All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no test of capacity competition for neurons.
All: polysemantic neurons are not measured.
All: no LLMs are studied, and neuron-level distribution is not measured.
All: one-dimensional and multi-dimensional features are not compared.

missing.what: Evolution of coverage, R2, F1 and ρuni over SAE training epochs (figure only, no numbers)
Correct ρuni values for the Table 2 CUB-R50 variants (Vanilla 0.1081, TopK 0.0828, Jump 0.1046, etc.). No row currently records them because the columns were misassigned.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label based on A5-subset is dropped. The paper expects most atoms to encode non-CBM factors (Prop. 4), and V5 does not claim every atom maps to a human concept. The tranche is changed from T5 to T3: vision-model SAEs are a new setting, and the paper offers no specific argument against V5 beyond cited non-identifiability. All Table 2 rows have mislabeled measures.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse feature co-activity, superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric phases are tested.
The paper varies SAE sparsity and expansion, but does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
No polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity are measured.
SAEs are evaluated on vision backbones, not LLMs; the paper does not measure how LLM activations are distributed across neurons.

The study tests SAE-to-CBM alignment as a proxy for semantic correspondence, not completeness or canonicality against ground-truth features, nor feature identity stability across independently trained dictionaries.
The study represents concepts as linear directions but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

relationships.condition: Trained SAEs on ResNet-50 / ViT / DINOv2 features, CUB and ImageNet, with CBM concepts as the reference
relationships.reason: How completely SAE dictionaries recover human concepts depends on design choices. Coverage (corrected columns) is 0.25 for TopK vs 0.73 for Jump (T2-TopK-rho, T2-Jump-rho). It runs 0.15–0.84 across sparsity (A4-L0-0012-cov, A4-L0-1000-cov) and 0.07–0.79 across expansion (A6-x1-cov, A6-x8-cov). Dictionaries are therefore not canonical or complete across settings.
relationships.display_finding: Coverage was 0.25 for TopK versus 0.73 for Jump, 0.15–0.84 across sparsity levels and 0.07–0.79 across expansion factors.

relation.reason: The study directly measures SAE recovery of independently supervised concept directions, bearing on V5 completeness.

tranche.reason: The results qualify V5 through incomplete and design-dependent recovery of reference concepts; this fits T5's explicit partial-claim definition.

source_check.notes: Coverage measures CBM-direction energy recovered through sparse nonnegative combinations, not a fraction of all model features. Random cones can inflate coverage; CBMs are partial references and complementary metrics are required.

statements.correction: Table 2, CUB–R50: TopK Coverage = 0.2548 ± 0.0450; Jump Coverage = 0.7320 ± 0.0427. CBMs are partial semantic references. Recovery depends on SAE design choices. V5 verdict: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The study-specific CUB coverage values are correct, but classifying this study as challenges overstates conditional, incomplete recovery.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that only a small subset of SAE atoms has strong CBM similarity and that most atoms align weakly or diffusely, which does not support treating every SAE atom as a complete canonical semantic unit (A5-subset).
